title: Odd One Out
source: MindSpark Grade 4 Aptitude & Reasoning | Chapter 2: Odd One Out
subtopics: Odd one out by category (animals, fruits, vehicles)
Odd one out by number property (even/odd, multiples)
Odd one out by letter property
learningGoals: Spot the one item that does not belong in a group.
Explain WHY an item is different using a clear reason.
Identify the common property shared by the other items.
coreIdeas: First, find what THREE of the four items have in common.
The item that does NOT share that common property is the odd one out.
Always give a reason — 'because all the others are...' makes your answer complete.

workedExamples.problem: Apple, Mango, Carrot, Banana — which is the odd one out?
workedExamples.solution: Apple, Mango, and Banana are all fruits. Carrot is a vegetable. So Carrot is the odd one out.

workedExamples.problem: 2, 4, 6, 7, 8 — which is the odd one out?
workedExamples.solution: 2, 4, 6, and 8 are all even numbers. 7 is an odd number. So 7 is the odd one out.

workedExamples.problem: Circle, Square, Triangle, Ball — which is the odd one out?
workedExamples.solution: Circle, Square, and Triangle are flat 2D shapes. Ball is a 3D object. So Ball is the odd one out.

onboarding.coachIntro: Spark the coach shows four everyday objects — three matching, one different — and asks: 'Which one does not belong?' to get the learner thinking visually. Then Spark explains the 'find the common thread' strategy before the first exercise.
onboarding.placementRule: Start at Group A for all learners. If two consecutive wrong answers occur in Groups A–B, walk through the three-step reasoning method again before continuing.

mission.missionPromise: By the end, you will always find the item that does not belong AND explain your reason like a true logic champion!
mission.successCelebration: Award a badge pulse and a coach cheer after every correct group. At lesson end, show 'Logic Lens' trophy.

microLessonPattern: Coach opens with a fun category hook.
Coach shows a worked group on the board and highlights the common property.
Coach reads the practice question aloud.
Student picks the odd one out and gives a reason.
Instant feedback praises or explains the common property.
Review question confirms mastery before next group.

rewardLoop.xpUnit: Award 10 to 20 XP per exercise group.
rewardLoop.streakRule: Show streak counter; protect with one free retry before streak breaks.
rewardLoop.badgeRule: Each group unlocks one badge tied to the category type.
rewardLoop.celebrationStyle: Quick coach praise + XP pulse + progress rail tick after every correct answer.

reviewLoop.trigger: Two incorrect attempts triggers a mini-reteach focusing on the common property of the three similar items.
reviewLoop.practiceStyle: Offer one easier follow-up question with more obvious differences.
reviewLoop.masteryRule: Advance only after a correct answer with a stated reason.
reviewLoop.revisitRule: Any group with two errors returns as a review card at the next session.

beats.teacherLine: Hey there, logic star! Today we play 'Odd One Out' — one of the most fun puzzles ever! You will see four things. Three of them share a secret — they all belong to the same group. But ONE of them is different, it sneaks in from a different group! Your job is to find the sneaky one and say WHY it does not belong. Ready to think like a detective?
beats.boardAction: Write 'Odd One Out' as the title. Below, list the 3-step method: Step 1 — Look at all four items. Step 2 — Find what THREE have in common. Step 3 — The fourth one is the odd one out!
beats.checkpointPrompt: Quick warm-up: Dog, Cat, Fish, Rose — which is the odd one out and why?
beats.expectedStudentResponse: Rose — because dog, cat, and fish are animals but rose is a flower/plant.
beats.fallbackHint: Dog, Cat, and Fish are all animals. Rose is a plant. The odd one out is Rose!

svgAnimation.text: Step 1: Look at all four items carefully
Step 2: Find what THREE of them share
Step 3: The one that does NOT share = Odd one out!

beats.teacherLine: Let me show you! Here are four things: Bus, Car, Truck, Bicycle. I ask myself: what do Bus, Car, and Truck have in common? They all have engines — they run on fuel! Bicycle has no engine; you pedal it. So Bicycle is the odd one out — because all the others have engines. See how I gave a reason? That is the key!
beats.boardAction: Write Bus, Car, Truck, Bicycle in a row. Circle Bus, Car, Truck and write 'have engines' below them. Draw a cross on Bicycle and write 'no engine — odd one out!'
beats.checkpointPrompt: Your turn: Sparrow, Crow, Eagle, Frog — which is the odd one out and why?
beats.expectedStudentResponse: Frog — because sparrow, crow, and eagle are birds but frog is not a bird.
beats.fallbackHint: Sparrow, Crow, and Eagle all have wings and can fly — they are birds. Frog is an amphibian, not a bird. So Frog is the odd one out!

svgAnimation.text: Bus, Car, Truck → have engines (run on fuel)
Bicycle → no engine → ODD ONE OUT!

beats.teacherLine: You know the three-step method. Now work through Groups A to F and find every odd one out! Remember: spotting it is half the job — giving a clear reason is the other half. Go for it, detective!
beats.boardAction: Show a mini cheatsheet: Types of properties to check — Category (what group?), Shape, Colour, Size, Number property, Letter property.
beats.checkpointPrompt: Before we start — if three items are red and one is blue, what is the odd one out's different property?
beats.expectedStudentResponse: Colour — the blue one is different in colour.
beats.fallbackHint: The three red items share the same colour. The blue one has a different colour — so colour is the property that makes it odd.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Odd one out by category (animals, fruits, vehicles)
sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's figure this out together! Three belong to the same family — one is an outsider. Find the outsider!

boardDemo.title: Category — Same Family?
steps: Items: Lion, Tiger, Elephant, Rose
Lion, Tiger, Elephant are animals
Rose is a flower (plant)
Odd one out: Rose — because all others are animals
boardDemo.teacherLine: Ask yourself: what group do three of these belong to? The one that does not fit that group is the odd one out!

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Look at: Mango, Banana, Orange, Potato — what category do three of them belong to?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Now you try: Bus, Car, Train, Chair — which one is the odd one out and why?
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Chair — because Bus, Car, and Train are vehicles but Chair is furniture.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: You nailed it! Bus, Car, Train are all vehicles for travelling. Chair is furniture. Great reasoning!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: Bus, Car, and Train all take you from one place to another — they are vehicles. Chair does not move you around — it is furniture!
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick check: Sparrow, Parrot, Pigeon, Dolphin — odd one out and reason?

visual.title: Odd One Out
visual.caption: Group A for Odd One Out.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's figure this out together! All shapes have sides, corners, and special properties. Find the shape that breaks the pattern!

boardDemo.title: Shape — Count the Sides
steps: Shapes: Square, Rectangle, Triangle, Circle
Square has 4 sides, Rectangle has 4 sides, Triangle has 3 sides
Circle has 0 sides — it is curved!
Odd one out: Circle — it is the only curved shape
boardDemo.teacherLine: Count the sides or look for curved vs straight edges. The shape with a different number of sides — or the only curved one — is the odd one out.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Look at these shapes: Pentagon (5 sides), Square (4 sides), Rectangle (4 sides), Rhombus (4 sides) — which one has a different number of sides?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: Triangle, Square, Circle, Rectangle — which is the odd one out?
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Circle — because Triangle, Square, and Rectangle are polygons with straight sides, but Circle is curved.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Perfect! Triangle, Square, and Rectangle all have straight sides. Circle is round with no sides. Circle is the odd one out!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: count the corners. Triangle has 3, Square has 4, Rectangle has 4 — they all have corners. Does a circle have any corners? No! So Circle is different.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: Circle, Oval, Sphere, Square — which is the odd one out?

visual.title: Odd One Out
visual.caption: Group B for Odd One Out.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's figure this out together! When colours group up, one stands alone. Find the colour that does not match the others!

boardDemo.title: Colour — Same Shade Family?
steps: Colours: Red, Orange, Yellow, Blue
Red, Orange, Yellow are warm colours
Blue is a cool colour
Odd one out: Blue — it is the only cool colour
boardDemo.teacherLine: Look for a shared colour property: same family (warm/cool), same darkness, or same type. The one that does not share the property is different.

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Look at: Green, Teal, Lime, Pink — which colour seems to be from a completely different colour family?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: Red, Blue, Green, Pink — three are primary colours. Which is NOT a primary colour and is the odd one out?
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Pink — because Red, Blue, and Green are primary colours but Pink is not.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Correct! Red, Blue, Green are the three primary colours in light. Pink is made by mixing — it is not a primary colour. Great eye!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: primary colours are the basic building-block colours. Red, Blue, Green (or in paints: Red, Blue, Yellow). Pink is a lighter shade of Red — not a primary colour on its own.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: White, Grey, Black, Orange — which is the odd one out? (Hint: think about shades vs bright colours.)

sessionFlow.subtopic: Odd one out by number property (even/odd, multiples)
sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's figure this out together! Numbers have families too — evens, odds, and multiples. Find the number that broke away from the family!

boardDemo.title: Number Property — Even or Odd?
steps: 12 is even, 18 is even, 24 is even
15 is odd (ends in 5)
Odd one out: 15 — it is the only odd number
boardDemo.teacherLine: Check each number: does it end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8 (even) or 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 (odd)? The one that breaks the pattern is the odd one out!

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Look at: 5, 10, 15, 12 — three are multiples of 5. Which one is NOT a multiple of 5?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: 2, 4, 7, 6 — which is the odd one out and why?
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: 7 — because 2, 4, and 6 are even numbers but 7 is odd.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Brilliant! 2, 4, 6 are all even numbers. 7 is an odd number — it does not belong with the evens!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: check the last digit. 2, 4, 6 all end in even digits. 7 ends in an odd digit. So 7 is the odd one out.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: 10, 20, 25, 30 — which is not a multiple of 10?

sessionFlow.subtopic: Odd one out by letter property
sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's figure this out together! Letters have properties too — vowels, consonants, and alphabet positions. Find the letter that does not belong!

boardDemo.title: Letters — Vowels vs Consonants
steps: Letters: A, E, I, B, O
A, E, I, O are vowels
B is a consonant
Odd one out: B — it is the only consonant
boardDemo.teacherLine: The five vowels are A, E, I, O, U. Every other letter is a consonant. When three or four vowels are together and one consonant sneaks in — that consonant is the odd one out!

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Look at: B, C, D, A — which is the odd one out? (Hint: think vowels and consonants.)
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: A, U, E, K — which is the odd one out and why?
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: K — because A, U, and E are vowels but K is a consonant.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Perfect! A, U, E are all vowels. K is a consonant. You know your vowels and consonants!
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: remember A, E, I, O, U are the five vowels. Everything else is a consonant. Check each letter — A, U, E are on the vowels list. K is not!
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Quick: P, Q, I, R — which is the odd one out?

visual.title: Odd One Out
visual.caption: Group E for Odd One Out.

sessionFlow.coachHook: Let's figure this out together! Sometimes three things are about the same size and one is much bigger or much smaller. Find the size outlier!

boardDemo.title: Size — Big or Small?
steps: Animals: Ant, Bee, Butterfly, Elephant
Ant, Bee, Butterfly are all small insects
Elephant is a huge animal
Odd one out: Elephant — it is much larger than the others
boardDemo.teacherLine: Compare sizes. If three things are small and one is huge — or three are big and one is tiny — the different-sized one is the odd one out!

sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Look at: Football, Tennis ball, Cricket ball, Bus — which one is very different in size?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Your turn: Pencil, Pen, Crayon, Building — which is the odd one out by size?
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: Building — because Pencil, Pen, and Crayon are small writing tools but a Building is enormous.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Exactly! Pencil, Pen, and Crayon all fit in your hand. A Building is huge! Building is clearly the odd one out by size.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Here's a trick: can you hold all four in your hand? Pencil — yes, Pen — yes, Crayon — yes, Building — no way! The one you cannot hold is the odd one out.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Final challenge: Sparrow, Eagle, Mountain, Crow — which is the odd one out by size?
